title: Making measurements in relativity
one_line_summary: Explains how an observer turns coordinate-free objects into laboratory numbers: the observer carries an orthonormal frame whose time axis is their own 4-velocity, components are read off by projection (giving E = -p.u), vielbein matrices translate between the coordinate bases used for calculation and the non-coordinate orthonormal bases where measurements happen, and two workhorse frames are built: the stationary frame of an observer at rest in the coordinates and the parallel-transported freely falling frame.
role_in_book: Placed between the connection and geodesic chapters (GA ch7-ch9) and the curvature chapter (GA ch11). Once geodesics and covariant derivatives can be computed in any coordinates, the book must say what a laboratory would actually record, taking Einstein's warning that coordinates have no built-in metric meaning as its theme. The tools introduced here are used straight away in §11.7 (tidal deviation in a falling frame) and then repeatedly: orthonormal fluid components (ch12), Robertson-Walker observers (ch16), static and infalling observers and photon energies in the Schwarzschild geometry (ch21-ch25), and the frame-based curvature calculations of Cartan's method in Part V (ch36). The authors mark everything from §10.2 onward as optional on a first pass, so the chapter doubles as a reference toolkit.

assumed_background.topic: 4-velocity, 4-momentum and the invariant dot product with signature (-,+,+,+)
Uniformly accelerated world line in Minkowski space with t and x as sinh and cosh of g tau
Plane polar coordinates, coordinate versus normalized basis vectors, and the commutator test for a coordinate basis
1-forms, basis 1-forms and the pairing <omega^mu, e_nu> = delta
Metric components as dot products of basis vectors; index raising and lowering
Equivalence principle, local inertial frames and the local flatness theorem
Covariant derivative along a curve, D/dtau notation, parallel transport, and Example 7.10 (flat case reduces to ordinary derivative)
Geodesics as free-fall world lines; connection coefficients and their non-tensorial transformation law (eqn 7.11)
Photon energy-frequency relation E = hbar omega and the wave vector
Kinematics in rotating polar unit vectors (centripetal and Coriolis-type terms)
Matrix products, inverses, diagonalization of symmetric matrices

learning_objectives: Reader can explain why a coordinate labelled t or r need not be a time or a distance, and how numbers acquire meaning only through an observer's local orthonormal frame.
Reader can obtain a measured component of any vector by dotting it with the observer's hatted basis vector, and raise or lower hatted indices with eta.
Reader can construct an observer's orthonormal frame by setting e_0hat equal to their 4-velocity and completing it with orthogonal unit spacelike vectors, as for the uniformly accelerated observer.

Reader can use E = -p.u_obs to compute the energy or frequency an observer measures, including gamma m for a moving observer and the exponential redshift omega exp(-g tau) seen by a uniformly accelerated observer.
Reader can distinguish a coordinate basis from a non-coordinate (orthonormal) basis and state the commutator test.
Reader can derive the radial and transverse acceleration components in a rotating orthonormal polar basis from the time derivatives of the unit vectors.
Reader can define vielbein components (e_alphahat)^mu and (e_mu)^alphahat, treat them as mutually inverse matrices, and use them to convert vector, 1-form and tensor components between frames.
Reader can state and check the defining relations g_{mu nu} = eta_{alphahat betahat} (e_mu)^alphahat (e_nu)^betahat and its inverse.
Reader can write down the stationary orthonormal frame for any diagonal metric by normalizing with 1/sqrt|g_mumu|, including the static observer in the Schwarzschild geometry.
Reader can transform a perfect-fluid energy-momentum tensor into orthonormal components and see it reduce to diag(rho, p, p, p).
Reader can define a freely falling frame by parallel transport of an orthonormal tetrad along a geodesic and build it for radial infall from rest at infinity in Schwarzschild.
Reader can show that in a freely falling frame the covariant proper-time derivative of a vector has frame components equal to ordinary derivatives of its frame components.

teaching_approach.summary: A toolkit chapter framed by a philosophical warning. It opens with Einstein's remark that coordinates lack direct metric meaning, then makes that concrete: a measurement is a projection onto an observer's own orthonormal axes, whose time axis is the observer's 4-velocity. A 2D momentum triangle and a world line decorated with little frames carry the picture; the first payoff, E = -p.u, is checked on a moving observer and on an accelerated observer seeing an exponential redshift. The authors then detour through a familiar Newtonian case (rotating polar unit vectors in the Kepler problem) to show why orthonormal bases are non-coordinate bases, and introduce vielbein components as the translation matrices. Almost everything is carried by short numbered examples with two-dimensional metrics (polar plane, unit sphere) before the payoff metrics (Schwarzschild static observer, perfect fluid, radial infall). Heavier 1-form justifications are pushed into margin notes, and there is an explicit skip-ahead sign for impatient readers.
narrative_arc: Motivating tension: GR lives in curved spacetime with arbitrary coordinates, but experiments are done locally in labs where spacetime looks Minkowskian; Einstein quote and slogan that coordinates carry no immediate metric meaning
Model of a measurement: a vector exists independently of coordinates; the observer projects it onto their hatted orthonormal axes (Fig. 10.1, Example 10.1)
Orienting the frame: the time basis vector equals the observer's 4-velocity (Fig. 10.2); remaining axes chosen orthogonal; worked for the uniformly accelerated observer (Example 10.2)
First payoff: measured energy E = -p.u_obs; checked for a particle seen by a moving observer (gamma m) and applied to starlight seen by the accelerated observer (exponential redshift, Example 10.3)
Complication announced: the natural orthonormal frame is a non-coordinate basis; optional-reading sign posted
Familiar illustration: normalized polar basis in the Kepler problem, where rotating unit vectors generate the r-theta-dot-squared and 2 r-dot theta-dot terms (Example 10.4, Fig. 10.3)
Formalism: coordinate basis dot products give g, orthonormal ones give eta; vielbein components translate components both ways (10.17-10.21), demonstrated on polar coordinates (Example 10.5)

Matrix view: vielbein as square matrix and its inverse on the unit sphere (Example 10.6); rules for swapping indices on vectors, 1-forms and tensors (10.38-10.40); defining relations boxed (10.41-10.42); 1-form justification in margin

First standard frame: stationary orthonormal frame of an observer at rest in the coordinates; orthonormality as a matrix equation (Example 10.8) and the square-root normalization recipe for diagonal metrics (Example 10.9, eqn 10.51)
Applications: static observer in Schwarzschild (Example 10.10); perfect-fluid stress tensor becomes diag(rho,p,p,p) in the orthonormal frame (Example 10.11)
Second standard frame: freely falling frame defined by parallel transport of the tetrad along a geodesic, motivated by the equivalence principle (eqn 10.60)
Application: tetrad for radial infall from rest at infinity in Schwarzschild (Example 10.12)
Consistency check: in the falling frame covariant derivatives of vectors become ordinary derivatives of frame components (Example 10.13), setting up geodesic deviation in ch11
signature_moves: Uses Einstein's own diagnosis of why GR took seven more years (coordinates are not measurements) as the organizing theme for a technical chapter.
Defines a measurement operationally as a dot product with the observer's basis vector, so that the sign in E = -p.u falls straight out of eta_00 = -1.
Identifies the observer's time axis with their 4-velocity and shows frames riding along a world line, making 'observer' a geometric object rather than a coordinate system.
Explains non-coordinate bases through a Newtonian problem the reader already knows (polar unit vectors in orbital mechanics) before any GR use.
Builds every vielbein first for a 2D metric (plane polar, unit sphere) where the matrices are diagonal and checkable by eye, then scales up to Schwarzschild.
Summarizes the vielbein as 'square roots of the metric components' for diagonal metrics, a compact working rule.
Records vielbein components for each metric in margin notes, a habit the book promises to continue in later chapters.
Places the 1-form derivation of the index-swapping rules in a long margin note, keeping the main line recipe-like while giving careful readers a proof.
Explicit reader-routing box telling curvature-hungry readers they can skip from §10.2 to ch11.

sections.title: Chapter opening: coordinates are not measurements
sections.summary: Opens with Einstein's reflection that the slow progress toward GR came from assuming coordinates must directly measure lengths and times. States that experiments are local, so an observer's small laboratory sees Minkowski spacetime, and that the link between curved-spacetime objects and laboratory numbers is the local orthonormal frame, whose components the book marks with hats and whose metric is diag(-1,1,1,1). Warns that labels such as t and r must not be read as time and radius until related to an observer's measurements; a margin note adds an H. G. Wells line about time as a fourth dimension.
concepts: coordinates have no immediate metrical significance
key_moves: Global curved stage versus local flat laboratory
Hatted indices introduced for orthonormal-frame components; eta_{muhat nuhat} = e_muhat . e_nuhat = diag(-1,1,1,1)
Slogan: coordinates acquire meaning only via local measurements

sections.title: Observers and their observations
sections.summary: A particle's momentum is a coordinate-free vector; an observer measures one of its components by dotting it with one of their orthonormal axes, which yields the lower-index component that eta can raise. The observer's axes are oriented by making the time basis vector equal to the observer's 4-velocity, with the spatial vectors chosen orthogonal and normalized; Example 10.2 carries this out for the uniformly accelerated observer, obtaining a boosted pair of cosh-sinh vectors. The energy an observer measures is then E = -p.u_obs, checked for a particle at rest viewed by a moving observer (E = gamma m) and applied to a photon from a star seen by the accelerated observer, whose measured frequency decays exponentially with proper time.

observer 4-velocity as the time basis vector
exponential redshift seen by a uniformly accelerated observer
key_moves: p . e_alphahat = p^muhat eta_{muhat alphahat} = p_alphahat (10.1)
e_0hat = u_obs, so the time axis has the components of the 4-velocity (10.2-10.3)
Accelerated observer: impose orthogonality (10.5) and normalization (10.6) to find e_1hat = (sinh g tau, cosh g tau, 0, 0) (10.7)
E = -p.u_obs = -p_0hat = p^0hat (10.8)
Moving observer: E = gamma m (10.9); photon: omega(tau) = omega exp(-g tau) (10.10)

sections.title: Coordinate and non-coordinate bases
sections.summary: Flagged as skippable on a first read. Recalls that polar coordinate basis vectors come from derivatives of Cartesian ones and have |e_theta| = r, whereas normalizing e_theta gives an orthonormal set that cannot be generated that way and whose members fail to commute: a non-coordinate basis. Example 10.4 shows such bases are natural in mechanics by differentiating rotating polar unit vectors to get the radial and transverse acceleration components. Calculations are usually done in coordinate bases (e_mu . e_nu = g) and measurements in orthonormal ones (e_alphahat . e_betahat = eta), so vielbein components are introduced as the matrices converting components between the two, with plane polar coordinates (Example 10.5) and the unit sphere (Example 10.6) as worked cases. General rules follow for converting upper and lower components and tensor components, the defining relations linking g and eta through the vielbein are boxed, a margin note justifies the rules using basis 1-forms, and Example 10.7 rederives E = -p.u in vielbein language.

metric as dot products of basis vectors

Vielbein matrices are inverses of each other (10.31)

sections.title: The orthonormal frame
sections.summary: Introduces the stationary orthonormal frame, belonging to an observer at rest with respect to the coordinates, whose 4-velocity has only a time component fixed by g_00 (u^0)^2 = -1. Margin notes establish it as the default frame whenever the book does not name an observer, and caution that its metric is Minkowskian but its connection coefficients need not vanish (that stronger property belongs to a local inertial frame). Finding the frame amounts to diagonalizing and normalizing the metric; Example 10.8 writes the condition as a matrix product for 1+1 dimensions, and Example 10.9 gives the recipe for diagonal metrics, summarized as vielbein components equal to reciprocal square roots (or square roots) of |g_mumu|. Example 10.10 applies it to the static observer in the Schwarzschild geometry and Example 10.11 converts a perfect-fluid energy-momentum tensor in a spherical-coordinate metric to orthonormal components, where it becomes diag(rho,p,p,p).

matrix form of the orthonormality condition
static observer frame in the Schwarzschild geometry
perfect-fluid energy-momentum tensor in an orthonormal frame

Diagonal metric: e_0hat = e_0/sqrt(-g_00), e_ihat = e_i/sqrt(g_ii) (10.48-10.49); (e_muhat)^mu = 1/sqrt|g_mumu| (10.51)
Schwarzschild static tetrad (10.53-10.55)

sections.title: Freely falling frames
sections.summary: Recalls from ch6 that a local inertial frame has Minkowski metric and vanishing first metric derivatives (hence vanishing connection) at a point, and singles out the freely falling frame as the most useful way to realize one: by the equivalence principle a small falling laboratory should see no gravity. The frame's time vector is the geodesic's 4-velocity, spatial vectors are chosen orthonormal to it at one event and parallel transported along the geodesic, so the frame is characterized by the covariant derivative of each basis vector along u vanishing (automatic for the time vector because the world line is a geodesic). Example 10.12 builds the tetrad for radial infall from rest at infinity in Schwarzschild, and Example 10.13, with a margin argument using parallel-transported basis 1-forms, shows that in this frame the components of D chi/d tau are simply the proper-time derivatives of the frame components of chi.

covariant derivative along a world line
covariant derivative reduces to ordinary derivative in a freely falling frame
key_moves: Equivalence principle motivates vanishing connection along the fall

Infall 4-velocity (10.61); diagonal choices for angular vectors; e_rhat fixed by normalization (10.62) with (e_rhat)^r = 1 (10.63)

Covariant derivative of a scalar is a directional derivative, giving (D chi/d tau)^muhat = d chi^muhat / d tau (10.69-10.71)

sections.title: Chapter summary and exercises
sections.summary: The summary lists five points: observers measure in orthonormal frames with e_0hat = u; the vielbein converts between frames; the stationary and freely falling frames are the two convenient choices; for a static observer u^0 = (-g_00)^{-1/2}; and diagonal-metric vielbein components are square roots of metric components. Seven exercises follow on orthonormal components in an open Robertson-Walker-type metric, orthonormal connection coefficients and commutators, radial motion seen by a local observer, gradient and divergence in orthogonal coordinates, the absence of frequency shift between points on a centrifuge rim, the Newman-Penrose null tetrad, and a vielbein for a light-cone metric.
key_moves: Summary restates u^0 = (-g_00)^{-1/2} and (e_i)^ihat = sqrt(g_ii)
Exercises extend to connection coefficients in a non-coordinate basis and to non-orthonormal (null) tetrads

concepts.name: coordinates have no immediate metrical significance
concepts.definition: Coordinate values in general relativity are arbitrary labels on events; a coordinate called t or r becomes a time or a distance only after it is related, through the metric, to intervals measured by some observer in their local frame.
concepts.how_introduced: Motivated by Einstein's remark that the delay in completing GR came from assuming coordinates directly measure lengths and times; stated as a slogan in the chapter opening and made operational by the orthonormal-frame machinery.
concepts.notes: Returns implicitly whenever the book later distinguishes coordinate speed dr/dt from locally measured speed (Exercise 10.3).

concepts.name: local orthonormal frame
concepts.definition: A set of four basis vectors e_alphahat at an event, one timelike and three spacelike, that are mutually orthogonal and unit-normalized, so that e_alphahat . e_betahat = eta_{alphahat betahat} = diag(-1,1,1,1). Components referred to it are what an observer carrying the frame measures, and hatted indices are raised and lowered with eta.
concepts.how_introduced: Introduced as the bridge between curved-spacetime objects and laboratory numbers, pictured first as ordinary 2D axes on which a momentum vector is resolved (Fig. 10.1), then as little frames carried along a world line (Fig. 10.2).
concepts.notes: The book notes the axes are 'usually' orthogonal; Exercise 10.6 shows a non-orthonormal (null) local basis as an alternative.

concepts.name: measurement as projection onto the observer's basis
concepts.definition: An observer measures the component of a vector along one of their axes by taking its dot product with that basis vector; because the frame metric is eta, this returns the lower-index frame component, and the upper-index component follows by raising with eta.
concepts.how_introduced: A particle's momentum passing through a lab is resolved on the lab's axes (Fig. 10.1) and Example 10.1 carries out the dot product.

concepts.name: observer 4-velocity as the time basis vector
concepts.definition: An observer's orthonormal frame is oriented so that its timelike basis vector coincides with the observer's 4-velocity, the unit tangent to their world line; the three spatial basis vectors are then any orthonormal triad perpendicular to it.
concepts.how_introduced: Argued from the fact that a clock at rest in the observer's lab moves through spacetime along the world line; drawn as frames along a curved world line (Fig. 10.2) and used in every later example.
concepts.notes: The spatial triad is fixed only up to a rotation; the book resolves this by convenient choices (aligning with coordinate directions) or, for falling frames, by parallel transport.

concepts.name: uniformly accelerated observer's orthonormal frame
concepts.definition: For an observer with constant proper acceleration g along x in Minkowski space, the frame is e_0hat = (cosh g tau, sinh g tau, 0, 0), e_1hat = (sinh g tau, cosh g tau, 0, 0), with e_2hat and e_3hat along y and z; it is a Lorentz boost with rapidity g tau that changes along the world line.
concepts.how_introduced: Example 10.2 revisits the hyperbolic world line from ch2, writes a trial e_1hat with two unknown functions and fixes them by orthogonality to u and unit normalization.
prerequisites: observer 4-velocity as the time basis vector
concepts.notes: The name Rindler is not used here; the example re-uses the letter g both for the acceleration and for an unknown component function.

concepts.name: energy measured by an observer
concepts.definition: The energy that an observer with 4-velocity u_obs assigns to a particle of 4-momentum p is the scalar E = -p.u_obs; since e_0hat = u_obs this is minus the lower time component in the observer's frame, which equals the upper time component because eta_00 = -1. The same rule with the wave vector gives the measured frequency.
concepts.how_introduced: Presented as a particularly handy tool right after the frame is oriented, proved in one line (10.8), tested on a particle at rest viewed by a moving observer (gamma m), and reproved in vielbein language in Example 10.7.
prerequisites: measurement as projection onto the observer's basis
observer 4-velocity as the time basis vector
concepts.notes: Because the right-hand side is a scalar it may be evaluated in any convenient frame (margin note 2). This is the single most reused result of the chapter, e.g. for gravitational redshift in Part IV.

concepts.name: wave 4-vector of light
concepts.definition: The 4-vector k with components (omega, k^x, k^y, k^z) describing a light wave, with omega = |k| for light in units c = 1; with hbar = 1 it doubles as the photon's 4-momentum, so an observer measures frequency omega = -k.u_obs.
concepts.how_introduced: Mentioned in a margin note to justify treating frequency exactly like energy in Example 10.3.

concepts.name: exponential redshift seen by a uniformly accelerated observer
concepts.definition: Light of frequency omega travelling along the direction of acceleration from a source at rest in an inertial frame is received by a uniformly accelerated observer with frequency omega exp(-g tau), decaying exponentially with the observer's proper time.
concepts.how_introduced: Second half of Example 10.3: plug the photon wave vector (omega, omega, 0, 0) and the accelerated 4-velocity into omega = -k.u, and combine cosh minus sinh into an exponential; a margin note links it to Hartle and to black-hole redshift in ch26-ch27.
concepts.notes: Equivalently a Doppler factor exp(-rapidity) with rapidity g tau. The chapter does not connect it to the accelerated observer's horizon, beyond which no signals ever reach them.

concepts.name: coordinate basis
concepts.definition: A basis whose vectors are the partial-derivative directions of a coordinate system, e_mu = d/dx^mu; its members commute and their dot products are the metric components g_{mu nu}, which in general are not those of eta.
concepts.how_introduced: Recalled from ch3 via plane polar coordinates, where |e_r| = 1 but |e_theta| = r because e_theta is built from derivatives of Cartesian components.

concepts.name: non-coordinate basis
concepts.definition: A basis of vector fields that is not the set of partial-derivative directions of any coordinate system; its members generally have non-zero commutators. Orthonormal frames in a curved or curvilinear setting are usually of this type.
concepts.how_introduced: Obtained by normalizing the polar e_theta to e_theta/r, which gives a frame convenient for measurements but not derivable from Cartesian coordinates; the commutator criterion from ch3 is quoted in a margin note. Framed as an 'unpleasant' property of observers' natural frames.
concepts.notes: The commutator value is from the book's Appendix E answer to Exercise 10.2, not the chapter text. In a non-coordinate basis the connection coefficients are no longer symmetric in their lower indices.

concepts.name: rotating orthonormal polar basis vectors
concepts.definition: For a point moving in a plane described with polar unit vectors, d e_rhat/dt = theta-dot e_thetahat and d e_thetahat/dt = -theta-dot e_rhat: each unit vector turns at the angular rate, the change being perpendicular to itself.
concepts.how_introduced: Example 10.4 differentiates r = r e_rhat twice for the Kepler problem, with Fig. 10.3 showing the two unit vectors at neighbouring angles and their difference vectors.

concepts.name: acceleration components in plane polar coordinates
concepts.definition: In the orthonormal polar frame the acceleration has radial component r-ddot minus r theta-dot squared (the second term being centripetal) and transverse component r theta-ddot plus 2 r-dot theta-dot (the second term being the Coriolis-like cross term).
concepts.how_introduced: Result of Example 10.4, used to show that non-coordinate bases are standard and useful in classical mechanics.
concepts.notes: The Kepler problem itself is treated in ch20.

concepts.name: metric as dot products of basis vectors
concepts.definition: The metric components in any basis are the dot products of its basis vectors; for a coordinate basis this gives g_{mu nu}, for an orthonormal frame it gives eta.
concepts.how_introduced: Recalled at the start of the vielbein discussion to set the two bases side by side (10.17-10.18).

concepts.name: vielbein
concepts.definition: The set of components (e_betahat)^alpha of the orthonormal basis vectors expressed in a coordinate basis, together with the inverse set (e_alpha)^betahat of coordinate basis vectors in the orthonormal basis. Each is a square matrix that converts vector components between the coordinate description and the orthonormal description.
concepts.how_introduced: Introduced as the translator needed because calculations are done in coordinate bases but measurements in orthonormal ones; the German name (many-legged, four-legged in spacetime) and a reading as 'making global coordinates local' are given in margin notes; worked for polar coordinates and the sphere.
concepts.notes: The bracket around e is decorative; e_mu^alphahat is an equivalent notation. The notation follows Hartle.

concepts.name: vielbein as an invertible matrix
concepts.definition: The matrix of coordinate-basis components in the orthonormal frame and the matrix of orthonormal components in the coordinate frame are inverses of each other, so contracting one with the other on either index gives a Kronecker delta.
concepts.how_introduced: Example 10.6 on the unit sphere writes the vielbein as a 2x2 matrix diag(1, sin theta) and inverts it to diag(1, 1/sin theta).
concepts.notes: For a diagonal metric the inverse is simply the reciprocal of each diagonal entry, with no summation implied (margin note 13).

concepts.name: vielbein transformation of tensor components
aliases: converting between hatted and unhatted indices
concepts.definition: Contracting with a vielbein trades a coordinate index for a frame index or vice versa, one index at a time: (e_muhat)^beta turns a lower coordinate index into a lower hatted one and an upper hatted index into an upper coordinate one, while (e_mu)^betahat does the reverse; a tensor needs one vielbein factor per index.
concepts.how_introduced: Stated as a general rule after Example 10.6, with a margin-note proof from the expansions of basis vectors and basis 1-forms, and applied to the fluid stress tensor in Example 10.11 and to the covariant derivative in Example 10.13.
formulas: (\boldsymbol e_{\hat\mu})^\beta p_\beta = p_{\hat\mu},\ (\boldsymbol e_{\hat\mu})^\beta p^{\hat\mu} = p^\beta
concepts.notes: Does not apply to connection coefficients, which are not tensors (hint to Exercise 10.2).

concepts.name: vielbein defining relations
concepts.definition: The metric in coordinates equals eta contracted with two copies of the vielbein, and conversely eta equals g contracted with two copies of the inverse vielbein; these relations are the conditions any proposed orthonormal frame must satisfy.
concepts.how_introduced: Boxed as the summary of §10.2; used as the check in Example 10.5 and as the equation to solve in §10.3 and Example 10.12.
concepts.notes: Given g, the vielbein is not unique: any local Lorentz transformation of the hatted index gives another valid frame, which is why the observer's 4-velocity must be specified.

concepts.name: orthonormal basis 1-forms
concepts.definition: The basis 1-forms omega^muhat dual to an orthonormal frame, satisfying <omega^muhat, e_nuhat> = delta; they are related to coordinate 1-forms by the vielbein and allow vielbein components to be written as pairings such as (e_nuhat)^mu = <omega^mu, e_nuhat>.
concepts.how_introduced: Used in margin note 10 to derive the index-swapping rules, in margin note 17 for the falling frame, and in the Example 10.13 margin argument; Exercise 10.6(b) asks for them for a null tetrad.
concepts.notes: Margin note stresses that <omega^mu, e_nuhat> is not a Kronecker delta because the two objects belong to different bases.

concepts.name: stationary orthonormal frame
aliases: orthonormal frame of an observer at rest in the coordinates
concepts.definition: The orthonormal frame carried by an observer whose spatial coordinates stay fixed, so their 4-velocity points along e_0 with u^0 = (-g_00)^{-1/2}; its time vector is e_0 rescaled to unit length and its spatial vectors are orthonormalized coordinate directions. Its metric is eta, but connection coefficients in it need not vanish.
concepts.how_introduced: Chosen as the natural frame for many later computations, particularly of curvature; margin notes make it the default whenever the book speaks of 'the orthonormal frame' without naming an observer, and contrast it with a local inertial frame.
prerequisites: observer 4-velocity as the time basis vector
concepts.notes: Exists only where g_00 < 0 (e.g. outside a Schwarzschild horizon, or within the light cylinder of a rotating frame); the chapter does not mention this restriction.

concepts.name: normalization of a static observer's 4-velocity
concepts.definition: For an observer at rest in the coordinates the only non-zero 4-velocity component is fixed by u.u = -1 to be the inverse square root of -g_00.
concepts.how_introduced: Example 10.9 and the chapter summary.
concepts.notes: The printed summary writes g_00 (u^0) = -1 without the square.

concepts.name: orthonormal frame for a diagonal metric
concepts.definition: When the metric is diagonal, the stationary orthonormal frame is obtained by dividing each coordinate basis vector by the square root of the absolute value of its metric component, so the non-zero vielbein components are 1/sqrt|g_mumu| and their inverses sqrt|g_mumu|.
concepts.how_introduced: Example 10.9 derives it from the normalization of u and checks it against the defining relation; the authors then phrase it as vielbein components being square roots of metric components, and apply it to Schwarzschild and to a spherical-coordinate metric.
concepts.notes: No sum over the repeated mu. For non-diagonal metrics (e.g. Exercise 10.5) one must orthogonalize, typically by Gram-Schmidt starting from e_0hat = u.

concepts.name: matrix form of the orthonormality condition
concepts.definition: Collecting the orthonormal basis-vector components into a matrix whose rows are the frame vectors, the conditions g(e_alphahat, e_betahat) = eta become the single matrix equation E g E^T = eta; finding a frame means finding such an E, i.e. diagonalizing and normalizing g.
concepts.how_introduced: Example 10.8 displays it for 1+1 dimensions without solving it, as a lead-in to the diagonal case.

concepts.name: Schwarzschild metric
concepts.definition: The vacuum geometry outside a spherically symmetric mass M, with line element -(1-2M/r) dt^2 + (1-2M/r)^{-1} dr^2 + r^2 dOmega^2 in units G = c = 1.
concepts.how_introduced: Quoted ahead of its derivation in ch21 as the prime example of a diagonal metric for which to build a static frame, and reused for radial infall in Example 10.12.
concepts.notes: Margin note 14 lists g_phiphi = r^2 sin theta, which should read r^2 sin^2 theta.

concepts.name: static observer frame in the Schwarzschild geometry
concepts.definition: For an observer at fixed r, theta, phi outside a Schwarzschild mass, the orthonormal frame is e_that = (1-2M/r)^{-1/2} e_t, e_rhat = (1-2M/r)^{1/2} e_r, e_thetahat = e_theta/r, e_phihat = e_phi/(r sin theta).
concepts.how_introduced: Example 10.10 applies the diagonal-metric normalization and verifies u.u = -1; inverse components listed in a margin note.
prerequisites: orthonormal frame for a diagonal metric
formulas: (\boldsymbol e_{\hat t})^t = (1-2M/r)^{-1/2},\ (\boldsymbol e_{\hat r})^r = (1-2M/r)^{1/2},\ (\boldsymbol e_{\hat\theta})^\theta = 1/r,\ (\boldsymbol e_{\hat\phi})^\phi = 1/(r\sin\theta)
concepts.notes: Used later to turn conserved quantities into locally measured energies (gravitational redshift) and to express Schwarzschild curvature in frame components (ch11 Exercise 11.2).

concepts.name: perfect-fluid energy-momentum tensor in an orthonormal frame
concepts.definition: A static perfect fluid whose coordinate components in a spherical-coordinate metric carry factors chi^2 and chi^2 sin^2 theta has, in the orthonormal frame, the simple rest-frame form T_{alphahat betahat} = diag(rho, p, p, p).
concepts.how_introduced: Example 10.11 converts one component explicitly with two vielbein factors and states the rest, as a demonstration of what vielbeins are for.
concepts.notes: The metric used is flat spacetime in spherical coordinates; the energy-momentum tensor itself is developed in ch12.

concepts.name: connection coefficients
concepts.definition: The coefficients describing how basis vectors change from point to point, which enter covariant derivatives; they are not tensor components, so they cannot be transformed with vielbeins, and they need not vanish in an orthonormal frame.
concepts.how_introduced: Relied on rather than developed: a margin note stresses the stationary frame can have non-zero connection coefficients, §10.4 seeks frames where they vanish, and Exercise 10.2 asks for them in an orthonormal polar frame.
prerequisites: covariant derivative along a world line
concepts.notes: The commutator relation (from Exercise 10.2b) holds when the first lower index is the direction of differentiation, which is the ordering used in the Appendix E answer; ch7 writes the derivative index last. In a coordinate basis the distinction is invisible because Gamma is symmetric.

concepts.name: local inertial frame
concepts.definition: Coordinates about an event in which the metric equals eta and all first derivatives of the metric vanish there, so that the connection coefficients vanish at that event; physics there looks like special relativity to first order.
concepts.how_introduced: Recalled from ch6 in margin note 12 (as the stronger requirement the stationary frame lacks) and at the start of §10.4 as the property freely falling frames are designed to have.

concepts.name: equivalence principle
concepts.definition: A sufficiently small freely falling laboratory cannot detect gravity by local experiments, so its natural coordinates behave as if the connection vanished.
concepts.how_introduced: Invoked in one sentence as the physical reason to expect a falling lab's frame to have vanishing connection coefficients.

concepts.name: geodesic
concepts.definition: A curve whose tangent vector is parallel transported along itself; freely falling bodies follow timelike geodesics, so u of a falling observer satisfies nabla_u u = 0.
concepts.how_introduced: Recalled as the world line of the falling laboratory; the fact that it is a geodesic is what makes nabla_u e_0hat = 0 automatic.

concepts.name: parallel transport
concepts.definition: Carrying a vector along a curve so that its covariant derivative along the tangent vanishes.
concepts.how_introduced: Used to extend an orthonormal triad chosen at one event along the whole free-fall geodesic.
prerequisites: covariant derivative along a world line

concepts.name: freely falling orthonormal frame
concepts.definition: An orthonormal frame carried along a timelike geodesic whose time vector is the geodesic's 4-velocity and whose basis vectors (and dual 1-forms) are all parallel transported along it, nabla_u e_alphahat = 0. It realizes, along the whole world line, the laboratory of a freely falling observer.
concepts.how_introduced: Motivated by the equivalence principle; defined by choosing a triad orthogonal to u at one event and parallel transporting; built explicitly for radial Schwarzschild infall and shown to turn covariant derivatives into ordinary ones.
prerequisites: observer 4-velocity as the time basis vector
concepts.notes: The text says the connection coefficients vanish along the geodesic; strictly, parallel transport guarantees only the coefficients whose differentiation direction is u; making all of them vanish on the world line requires Fermi normal coordinates (Fermi transport appears in GA Exercise 32.2). A ch6 summary point describes the same frame as flat only in a small spatial region but for long proper times.

concepts.name: infalling observer frame in the Schwarzschild geometry
concepts.definition: For radial fall from rest at infinity, u^alpha = [(1-2M/r)^{-1}, -(2M/r)^{1/2}, 0, 0]; the frame has e_that = u, e_rhat = (-(2M/r)^{1/2}(1-2M/r)^{-1}, 1, 0, 0), e_thetahat = e_theta/r and e_phihat = e_phi/(r sin theta).
concepts.how_introduced: Example 10.12 takes the 4-velocity from ch22, keeps the angular vectors diagonal as before, and fixes e_rhat from its normalization with its r component set to 1.
concepts.notes: Own check: e_rhat is orthogonal to u and unit, and together with e_thetahat, e_phihat is indeed parallel transported along the radial geodesic. Relative to the static frame this frame is boosted inward with speed (2M/r)^{1/2} and gamma = (1-2M/r)^{-1/2}.

concepts.name: covariant derivative along a world line
concepts.definition: The rate of change of a vector along a curve with tangent u, including the change of the basis vectors: (D V/dtau)^mu = u^alpha(partial_alpha V^mu + Gamma^mu_{alpha nu} V^nu); on a scalar it reduces to the directional derivative u^alpha partial_alpha f.
concepts.how_introduced: Recalled in Example 10.13, where the book points back to Example 7.10 (flat Cartesian case) and generalizes that result to any freely falling frame.

concepts.name: covariant derivative reduces to ordinary derivative in a freely falling frame
concepts.definition: In a parallel-transported orthonormal frame the hatted components of the covariant derivative of any vector along the world line equal the ordinary proper-time derivatives of its hatted components, because the frame vectors themselves do not change along the curve.
concepts.how_introduced: Example 10.13: pull the vielbein into the covariant derivative using the parallel-transported basis 1-forms (margin note 18), recognize a scalar, and use the chain rule.
prerequisites: covariant derivative along a world line
concepts.notes: Sets up ch11 §11.7, where D^2 xi/dtau^2 becomes an ordinary second derivative in the geodesic deviation equation.

concepts.name: Newman-Penrose null tetrad
concepts.definition: A local basis of two real null vectors l and n and two complex-conjugate null vectors m and m-bar, with l.n and m.m-bar the only non-zero products, used instead of an orthonormal frame; the local metric in this basis is off-diagonal.
concepts.how_introduced: Only in Exercise 10.6, as an alternative to orthonormal bases.
concepts.notes: The normalization signs quoted suit a (+,-,-,-) signature, unlike the rest of the book; a learner working in (-,+,+,+) would usually take l.n = -1 and m.m-bar = +1.

concepts.name: commutator of vector fields
concepts.definition: For vector fields viewed as derivative operators, [u, v] = uv - vu; coordinate basis vectors commute, while normalized curvilinear basis vectors generally do not.
concepts.how_introduced: Cited in margin note 5 from ch3 as the test that identifies a non-coordinate basis; needed in Exercise 10.2(b).
formulas: [\boldsymbol u,\boldsymbol v] = \boldsymbol u\boldsymbol v - \boldsymbol v\boldsymbol u

concepts.name: 4-momentum
concepts.definition: The coordinate-independent 4-vector p = m u of a particle, whose time component in a given frame is the energy measured there.
concepts.how_introduced: Used as the running example of a vector an observer measures.

worked_examples.label: Example 10.1
worked_examples.problem: Show what an observer obtains by dotting a momentum vector with one of their frame vectors.
worked_examples.method: Expand p in the hatted basis, use e_muhat . e_alphahat = eta, and raise the index with the inverse Minkowski metric if the upper component is wanted.
worked_examples.key_insight: Projection gives the lower-index component directly; in an orthonormal frame raising or lowering only flips the sign of the time component.
worked_examples.result: p . e_alphahat = p_alphahat; p^betahat = eta^{alphahat betahat} p_alphahat.
concepts: measurement as projection onto the observer's basis

worked_examples.label: Example 10.2
worked_examples.problem: Construct the full orthonormal frame of the uniformly accelerated observer of ch2.
worked_examples.method: Take e_0hat as the known 4-velocity (cosh g tau, sinh g tau, 0, 0); put e_2hat and e_3hat along y and z; write e_1hat with two unknown t and x components and impose orthogonality to e_0hat and unit normalization.
worked_examples.key_insight: The spatial axis is the Minkowski 'mirror image' of the time axis: swapping cosh and sinh; the frame is a boost whose rapidity grows linearly with proper time.
worked_examples.result: e_1hat = (sinh g tau, cosh g tau, 0, 0), e_2hat = (0,0,1,0), e_3hat = (0,0,0,1).
concepts: observer 4-velocity as the time basis vector

worked_examples.label: Example 10.3
worked_examples.problem: (i) Find the energy of a particle at rest as measured by an observer moving with speed v. (ii) Find the frequency of starlight measured by the uniformly accelerated observer.
worked_examples.method: Evaluate the scalar -p.u_obs in the particle's rest frame with u_obs = (gamma, gamma v, 0, 0); then evaluate -k.u_obs with k = (omega, omega, 0, 0) and the accelerated 4-velocity, using cosh x - sinh x = exp(-x).
worked_examples.key_insight: Because -p.u is a scalar, pick whichever frame makes the arithmetic trivial; the same one-line formula yields relativistic energy and Doppler shifts.
worked_examples.result: E = gamma m (gamma m c^2 with c restored); omega(tau) = omega exp(-g tau), an exponentially growing redshift.
concepts: exponential redshift seen by a uniformly accelerated observer

worked_examples.label: Example 10.4
worked_examples.problem: Derive the velocity and acceleration components of a particle in an orthonormal polar basis (Kepler problem setting).
worked_examples.method: Differentiate r = r e_rhat, remembering that the unit vectors rotate: d e_rhat/dt = theta-dot e_thetahat and d e_thetahat/dt = -theta-dot e_rhat (Fig. 10.3); collect terms along each unit vector.
worked_examples.key_insight: Extra terms in the acceleration are not forces but consequences of a basis that changes from place to place; this is a classical preview of connection coefficients in a non-coordinate basis.
worked_examples.result: a^rhat = r-ddot - r theta-dot^2; a^thetahat = r theta-ddot + 2 r-dot theta-dot.
concepts: acceleration components in plane polar coordinates

worked_examples.label: Example 10.5
worked_examples.problem: Set up vielbein components between the coordinate basis and the orthonormal basis for the flat plane in polar coordinates, and verify orthonormality.
worked_examples.method: Read g_rr = 1 and g_thetatheta = r^2 from the line element; choose e_rhat = e_r and e_thetahat = e_theta/r; write the trivial self-components, then the cross components (e_thetahat)^theta = 1/r and (e_theta)^thetahat = r; check with g_{alpha beta}(e_muhat)^alpha (e_nuhat)^beta = eta.
worked_examples.key_insight: The only non-trivial vielbein entries are the scale factors; checking a frame means contracting with g, not with eta.

worked_examples.label: Example 10.6
worked_examples.problem: Write the vielbein for the unit-sphere metric as a matrix and find its inverse.
worked_examples.method: Normalize the diagonal metric d theta^2 + sin^2 theta d phi^2 to get (e_mu)^alphahat = diag(1, sin theta); use the matrix inverse relations to get (e_alphahat)^mu = diag(1, 1/sin theta).
worked_examples.key_insight: Vielbeins are ordinary square matrices, so inverse relations are just matrix inversion; for diagonal metrics it is entry-by-entry reciprocals.

worked_examples.label: Example 10.7
worked_examples.problem: Show that the vielbein formalism reproduces E = -p.u_obs.
worked_examples.method: Write the dot product with g, lower the index on p, recognize (e_0hat)^nu p_nu as the hatted component p_0hat via the index-swap rule, then raise with eta_00 = -1.
worked_examples.key_insight: The observer-energy rule is just the vielbein rule applied to the time index, guaranteed by choosing e_0hat = u_obs.

worked_examples.label: Example 10.8
worked_examples.problem: Express the orthonormality condition as a matrix equation in 1+1 dimensions.
worked_examples.method: Arrange frame components as a matrix E (rows = frame vectors) and write E g E^T = diag(-1, 1).
worked_examples.key_insight: Finding a frame is a matrix congruence problem: diagonalize the symmetric metric and rescale to plus or minus one.
concepts: matrix form of the orthonormality condition

worked_examples.label: Example 10.9
worked_examples.problem: Find the stationary orthonormal frame for a general diagonal metric.
worked_examples.method: Normalize the static 4-velocity, g_00 (u^0)^2 = -1, set e_0hat = u, then divide each spatial coordinate vector by the square root of its metric component; verify with the defining relation.
worked_examples.key_insight: For diagonal metrics no diagonalization is needed; the vielbein is the square root of the metric entry by entry.
concepts: orthonormal frame for a diagonal metric

worked_examples.label: Example 10.10
worked_examples.problem: Find the orthonormal frame of an observer at rest in the Schwarzschild geometry.
worked_examples.method: Apply the diagonal-metric recipe to the four Schwarzschild metric components and confirm u.u = -1.
worked_examples.key_insight: Static observers' clocks and rulers are the coordinate ones rescaled by the gravitational factors (1-2M/r)^{-/+1/2}, which will later give gravitational time dilation and redshift.
worked_examples.result: e_that = (1-2M/r)^{-1/2} e_t, e_rhat = (1-2M/r)^{1/2} e_r, e_thetahat = e_theta/r, e_phihat = e_phi/(r sin theta).
concepts: static observer frame in the Schwarzschild geometry
orthonormal frame for a diagonal metric

worked_examples.label: Example 10.11
worked_examples.problem: Convert a static perfect fluid's energy-momentum tensor from coordinate to orthonormal components in flat spherical coordinates.
worked_examples.method: Use the diagonal vielbein, one factor per index, e.g. multiply T_thetatheta = p chi^2 by (1/chi)^2.
worked_examples.key_insight: Orthonormal components strip out the coordinate scale factors, exposing the physical density and isotropic pressure.
worked_examples.result: T_{thatthat} = rho and all three spatial diagonal components equal p.
concepts: perfect-fluid energy-momentum tensor in an orthonormal frame

worked_examples.label: Example 10.12
worked_examples.problem: Build the freely falling frame of an observer falling radially from rest at infinity in Schwarzschild.
worked_examples.method: Set e_that = u from the known infall 4-velocity; keep the angular frame vectors diagonal as for the static observer; solve the normalization of e_rhat within the t-r plane with its r component taken as 1.
worked_examples.key_insight: A falling frame mixes t and r components: it is the static frame boosted inward, so its radial vector acquires a time component.
concepts: infalling observer frame in the Schwarzschild geometry

worked_examples.label: Example 10.13
worked_examples.problem: Show that in a freely falling frame the frame components of D chi/d tau are ordinary derivatives d chi^muhat/d tau.
worked_examples.method: Write the frame component of nabla_u chi as a pairing with omega^muhat; use the Leibniz rule and nabla_u omega^muhat = 0 to move the derivative outside; treat chi^muhat as a scalar whose covariant derivative is u^beta partial_beta; apply the chain rule.
worked_examples.key_insight: Parallel-transported frames make the frame vectors behave like constant Cartesian axes along the world line, generalizing Example 7.10 to curved spacetime.
concepts: covariant derivative reduces to ordinary derivative in a freely falling frame

worked_examples.problem: Exercise 10.3 (answer in Appendix E): coordinate versus locally measured radial speed for a particle with conserved u_t = a in a static spherically symmetric field.
worked_examples.method: Use u.u = -1 with the diagonal metric to get u^r, form dr/dt = u^r/u^t, then convert time and radial intervals to the static observer's frame with the diagonal vielbein.
worked_examples.key_insight: Coordinate speed is not what anyone measures; the local observer's speed involves sqrt(g_rr/(-g_tt)) and simplifies to a formula in g_tt and a alone.
worked_examples.result: d rhat/d that = sqrt(1 + g_tt/a^2), with dr/dt = g_tt u^r / a on the way (Appendix E, E.93-E.94; re-derived independently).
concepts: orthonormal frame for a diagonal metric
coordinates have no immediate metrical significance

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: Resolving a 2D arrow on a set of drawn axes
analogies_and_intuitions.target_concept: measurement as projection onto the observer's basis
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: The familiar picture of splitting a planar vector into components along x-hat and y-hat stands in for an observer extracting energy and momentum along four spacetime axes.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Euclidean projection hides the minus sign of eta_00: in spacetime the time component obtained by dotting with e_0hat is minus the energy, and boosted axes do not look perpendicular on a diagram.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Morph the Euclidean picture into a Minkowski diagram as a 'signature' slider moves from + to -, so learners see where the sign flip enters.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: An observer as a clock-carrying laboratory whose clock ticks along the world line
analogies_and_intuitions.target_concept: observer 4-velocity as the time basis vector
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: A clock at rest in the lab moves through spacetime along the world line, so the lab's time axis must point along the tangent.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Says nothing about how to orient the spatial axes; a rotating lab and a non-rotating lab share the same e_0hat.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Clock-and-rulers glyph attached to a world line in a spacetime diagram, with a gyroscope option that distinguishes parallel-transported from rotating spatial axes.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: Vielbein components as square roots of the metric
analogies_and_intuitions.target_concept: orthonormal frame for a diagonal metric
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Since g = e^T eta e, for a diagonal metric each vielbein entry is the square root of the corresponding |g_mumu|, like taking a matrix square root.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Only literally true for diagonal metrics; in general a vielbein is a non-unique matrix 'square root' defined up to Lorentz transformations, and off-diagonal metrics need orthogonalization.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Metric-to-vielbein calculator: enter a 2x2 or 4x4 metric; diagonal cases show square roots; non-diagonal cases animate Gram-Schmidt from e_0hat = u.

analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Margin note suggests picturing the coordinate frame as global labels such as (t, r, theta, phi), with the vielbein converting them into the local rulers and clocks of an observer.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: The vielbein acts on tangent vectors at a point, not on the coordinates themselves; there are generally no coordinates whose basis is the orthonormal frame.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: Rotating unit vectors in orbital mechanics
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: The Kepler-problem habit of using e_rhat and e_thetahat shows that non-coordinate bases are everyday tools, and that their turning produces extra acceleration terms.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: In the plane the non-commutation is a coordinate artefact of flat space; it does not by itself signal curvature or a gravitational field.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Orbit sandbox where the learner sees a^rhat and a^thetahat split into 'real force' and 'basis turning' parts for an elliptical Kepler orbit.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: A small falling laboratory sees no gravity, like carrying fixed Cartesian axes
analogies_and_intuitions.target_concept: covariant derivative reduces to ordinary derivative in a freely falling frame
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Equivalence-principle intuition motivates choosing parallel-transported axes, along which the frame vectors behave as if constant, so derivatives of components are the whole story.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Holds only along the world line and to first order away from it; tidal effects (curvature) appear at second order, which is the subject of ch11.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Elevator-in-free-fall view next to a coordinate view of the same world line near a mass, with frame arrows that never twist in the elevator view.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: Time Traveller's remark that time differs from space only because consciousness moves along it
analogies_and_intuitions.target_concept: coordinates have no immediate metrical significance
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: A literary margin note (H. G. Wells) that dramatizes the geometric view of time as a coordinate direction.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Decorative; it can even encourage the misreading that a coordinate labelled t is automatically time.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: A coordinate named t is a time and a coordinate named r is a radius or distance.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Coordinates are labels; physical times and lengths come from the metric evaluated in some observer's local orthonormal frame (e.g. static-observer proper time is sqrt(-g_tt) dt).
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Coordinate names are chosen by analogy with flat space, and in weak fields the numbers nearly agree.
concepts: coordinates have no immediate metrical significance

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Energy is simply the time component p^0 of the momentum in whatever coordinates are being used.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Energy is observer-dependent: it is -p.u_obs, i.e. the time component in that observer's orthonormal frame; coordinate components p^t are not energies unless the coordinate frame happens to be that observer's orthonormal frame.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: In special relativity with inertial Cartesian coordinates p^0 is the energy, so the habit transfers.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Any orthonormal frame is a local inertial frame, so its connection coefficients vanish.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Orthonormality only makes the metric Minkowskian at the point; vanishing connection (first metric derivatives) is an extra condition met, along a geodesic, by the freely falling frame.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Both kinds of frame have eta as their metric, and 'local frame' is used loosely for both.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Connection coefficients can be transformed to an orthonormal frame with vielbeins like any other indexed object.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: They are not tensor components; they must be computed from how the frame vectors change, or transformed with an inhomogeneous law.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Every other object in the chapter converts index by index with vielbein factors.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: An orthonormal basis must be a coordinate basis, since normalized polar unit vectors look like they come from polar coordinates.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Normalized basis vectors such as e_theta/r are generally not derivative directions of any coordinates; their commutator is non-zero.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Undergraduate vector calculus uses r-hat and theta-hat alongside (r, theta) without distinguishing the two notions.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: The vielbein relation <omega^mu, e_nuhat> is a Kronecker delta, like the duality relation for a single basis.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Pairing a coordinate 1-form with a frame vector gives the vielbein component (e_nuhat)^mu, which differs from delta because the two belong to different bases.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Index patterns look identical to <omega^mu, e_nu> = delta once hats are overlooked (hats are easily lost in handwriting and OCR).

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Extra terms like -r theta-dot^2 in polar acceleration are real forces.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: They arise from the rotation of the unit vectors used to express the acceleration; the geometric acceleration vector is unchanged.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: In mechanics courses these terms are often called centrifugal and Coriolis forces.
concepts: acceleration components in plane polar coordinates

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: There is a single 'correct' orthonormal frame at each event.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Frames are fixed only once an observer's 4-velocity is chosen and a spatial orientation picked; static and infalling observers at the same event have different frames related by a boost.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: The chapter speaks of 'the orthonormal frame' and a margin note makes the static frame the default.
concepts: infalling observer frame in the Schwarzschild geometry

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Static observers can be placed anywhere in a geometry, e.g. at any r in Schwarzschild.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: A static frame requires g_00 < 0; at and inside r = 2M (or beyond the light cylinder in a rotating frame) no observer can stay at fixed spatial coordinates and u^0 = (-g_00)^{-1/2} is undefined.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: The recipe u^0 = (-g_00)^{-1/2} is presented without its domain of validity.
concepts: static observer frame in the Schwarzschild geometry

thought_experiments.name: Particle crossing a laboratory
thought_experiments.setup: A particle with momentum p passes through a lab whose observer carries orthonormal axes; the observer wants its energy and momentum components.
thought_experiments.lesson: Measurement is the projection of a frame-independent vector onto the observer's own axes; different observers get different components of the same vector.
concepts: measurement as projection onto the observer's basis
thought_experiments.app_idea: Several labs with different velocities at the same event, each displaying its own readout of the same particle's E and p.

thought_experiments.name: Accelerating rocket watching a star
thought_experiments.setup: A rocket with constant proper acceleration heads directly away from a star that is at rest in an inertial frame, so the starlight catches up with it from behind along the line of motion. The crew records the frequency they receive as their proper time goes on.
thought_experiments.lesson: The received frequency falls exponentially, omega exp(-g tau); this is the flat-space prototype of the exponential redshift of light from near a black-hole horizon.
concepts: exponential redshift seen by a uniformly accelerated observer
thought_experiments.app_idea: Rindler diagram with incoming null rays from the star and a colour-shifting star image in the rocket window versus proper time; slider for g.

thought_experiments.name: Small laboratory in free fall around a mass
thought_experiments.setup: A sealed lab falls freely along a geodesic; its occupants set up axes at one moment and keep them non-rotating.
thought_experiments.lesson: By the equivalence principle their frame is parallel transported and locally inertial along the fall, so derivatives of frame components behave as in special relativity.
concepts: covariant derivative reduces to ordinary derivative in a freely falling frame
thought_experiments.app_idea: Side-by-side: static hovering observer and infalling observer at the same r in Schwarzschild, with frame arrows on a t-r diagram showing the relative boost of speed sqrt(2M/r).

thought_experiments.name: Signal around a centrifuge rim (Exercise 10.5)
thought_experiments.setup: A source and a detector sit on the rim of a spinning centrifuge, separated by an angle; light is sent from one to the other.
thought_experiments.lesson: Both are static in the rotating (stationary) metric at the same radius, so they measure the same frequency: rotation-induced shifts depend on radius, not on angular separation.
thought_experiments.app_idea: Spinning disk with draggable source and detector; readout of emitted and received frequency showing a shift only when their radii differ.

historical_notes.event: Recollection (in the Schilpp volume 'Albert Einstein: Philosopher-Scientist', cited by the book in its 1969 edition) that the years between special and general relativity were largely spent freeing himself from the belief that coordinates must carry direct metric meaning.
historical_notes.significance: Frames the whole chapter: the operational link between coordinates and measurement is exactly what the orthonormal-frame machinery supplies.

historical_notes.event: The Time Machine's narrator describes time as a fourth dimension differing from space only through our motion along it (quoted in margin note 1).
historical_notes.significance: Literary precursor of the spacetime view; used as colour rather than physics.

historical_notes.event: Introduced a null tetrad formalism (two real and two complex null vectors) as an alternative to orthonormal frames.
historical_notes.significance: Standard tool for radiation and black-hole perturbation problems; appears here only in Exercise 10.6.

historical_notes.event: Credited in margin notes as the source of the vielbein notation and of the accelerated-observer redshift discussion.
historical_notes.significance: Points the reader to a gentler, physics-first companion text.

applications_and_observations.topic: Relativistic energy of a moving particle
applications_and_observations.details: Measured energy of a particle at rest seen by an observer moving at speed v follows from E = -p.u.

applications_and_observations.topic: Exponential redshift for a uniformly accelerated observer
applications_and_observations.details: Frequency received from a star by an observer with constant proper acceleration g decays as exp(-g tau). Own estimate: for g = 9.8 m/s^2 the e-folding proper time is c/g, roughly 3.06e7 s or about 0.97 yr.
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: omega(tau) = omega exp(-g tau/c) with c restored; c/g ~ 0.97 yr at 1 g (own estimate).

applications_and_observations.topic: Kepler problem in orthonormal polar components
applications_and_observations.details: Radial and transverse acceleration components used for planetary orbits come from differentiating rotating unit vectors; full treatment in ch20.
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: a^rhat = r-ddot - r theta-dot^2, a^thetahat = r theta-ddot + 2 r-dot theta-dot.

applications_and_observations.topic: Static observers outside a spherical mass (Schwarzschild)
applications_and_observations.details: Clocks of static observers run at sqrt(1-2M/r) of coordinate time, and radial rulers are stretched by (1-2M/r)^{-1/2}. Own estimate using E = -p.u: a photon from infinity is blueshifted by (1-2GM/rc^2)^{-1/2}; at the Earth's surface 2GM/rc^2 is about 1.4e-9, giving a fractional shift near 7e-10; at a neutron-star surface (M ~ 1.4 solar masses, r ~ 12 km) 2GM/rc^2 is about 0.34, giving a factor near 1.23.
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: (e_that)^t = (1-2M/r)^{-1/2}; Earth surface shift ~7e-10; neutron star factor ~1.23 (own estimates).

applications_and_observations.topic: Perfect fluid seen in an orthonormal frame
applications_and_observations.details: Coordinate components of a fluid's stress tensor carry metric factors; in the orthonormal frame they reduce to density and isotropic pressure, the form used for stars and cosmology.
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: T_{alphahat betahat} = diag(rho, p, p, p).

applications_and_observations.topic: Radial free fall into a Schwarzschild black hole
applications_and_observations.details: Frame of an observer dropped from rest at infinity; with ch11 it gives the tidal stretching felt on the way in. Own derivation: relative to a static observer at the same r the infaller moves inward at the Newtonian escape speed sqrt(2M/r), reaching the speed of light only at r = 2M, where static observers cease to exist.
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: u^r = -(2M/r)^{1/2}; local relative speed sqrt(2M/r) (own derivation).

applications_and_observations.details: Exercise 10.5 shows no frequency shift between emitter and detector on the same rim of a rotating centrifuge, since both are static in the stationary rotating metric at the same radius (Appendix E reasoning). Rotor experiments of this kind with Mossbauer sources (e.g. Hay, Schiffer, Cranshaw and Egelstaff, 1960) test the transverse Doppler effect when source and absorber are at different radii; this historical link is not made in the book.
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: Shift factor depends on (1 - Omega^2 r^2)^{1/2} at each radius; zero for equal radii.

notation_and_conventions.convention: Components in a local orthonormal frame carry hats (e_alphahat, p^muhat); hatted indices are raised and lowered with eta = diag(-1,1,1,1). Coordinate-frame indices are unhatted.
notation_and_conventions.notes: Hats are frequently lost or garbled in the reading copy; the rendered pages are reliable.

notation_and_conventions.convention: Signature (-,+,+,+); c = 1 (restored as gamma m c^2 in Example 10.3); hbar = 1 for photons; G = 1 in Schwarzschild expressions.
notation_and_conventions.notes: Exercise 10.6 uses Newman-Penrose normalizations natural in (+,-,-,-).

notation_and_conventions.convention: (e_betahat)^alpha is the alpha coordinate component of the betahat frame vector; (e_alpha)^betahat is the betahat frame component of the alpha coordinate vector. The bracket is decorative and e_alpha^betahat means the same. Follows Hartle.
notation_and_conventions.notes: Vielbein components for each metric are recorded in margin notes throughout the book.

notation_and_conventions.item: No summation on mixed hatted/unhatted repeats
notation_and_conventions.convention: In expressions such as (e_mu)^muhat = 1/(e_muhat)^mu or g_mumu (e_0hat)^mu (e_0hat)^mu, an index appearing with and without a hat is not summed.
When the book refers to 'the orthonormal frame' without naming an observer, it means the frame of an observer at rest in the coordinate system.
D V/dtau denotes nabla_u V, the covariant derivative along the world line; its components are written (D V/dtau)^mu.
Indices are written as numbers (0,1,2,3 or 1,2 in 2D examples) or as coordinate names (t, r, theta, phi, chi) interchangeably, e.g. e_that = e_0hat.

notation_and_conventions.item: Local metric symbols for general tetrads
notation_and_conventions.convention: In Exercise 10.6 the local metric for a null tetrad is still written eta_{muhat nuhat} (overbars in the print), although it is no longer diag(-1,1,1,1).

margin_notes.summary: Wells' Time Traveller on time as a dimension like space except for our movement along it, offered as a memorable variant of the chapter's warning about coordinates.
Because -p.u is a scalar it can be evaluated in the particle's rest frame and trusted in every frame.
Wave-vector components (omega, k) with omega = |k| for light; E = hbar omega with hbar set to 1.
The exponential redshift result is discussed by Hartle and returns in the black-hole chapters 26 and 27.
Reader-routing box: the remainder of the chapter details bases and transformations and may be skipped on a first pass by readers eager to reach curvature in ch11.
Recalled from ch3: non-coordinate basis vectors fail to commute, whereas coordinate basis vectors commute.
The Kepler problem is treated in ch20.
Etymology of vielbein (German 'many legs') and vierbein (four legs) for 3+1 dimensions; the bracket in (e_mu)^alphahat is cosmetic.
Picture a vielbein as the device that turns global coordinates such as (t, r, theta, phi) into local ones.
Notation follows Hartle; the book will list vielbein components in margins for later metrics; polar-plane components given.
Vielbein components for the unit sphere: 1 for theta, sin theta for phi.

Long 1-form justification of the vielbein rules: expansions of frame vectors and 1-forms (10.33), recovering components by pairing with basis 1-forms (10.34-10.37), with a caution that a mixed pairing is not a Kronecker delta.

Note 11 (missing from the reading copy, recovered from the render): from here on, whenever the book says 'the orthonormal frame' and names no observer, read it as the frame of someone sitting still in the coordinates.
Note 12 (recovered from the render): the stronger object is a LIF, where the connection also vanishes at the chosen point; the authors postpone that stricter frame to §10.4.
Note 13 (recovered from the render): the summation convention is suspended for an index that appears once with a hat and once without.
Boxed pointer beside Example 10.10: the Schwarzschild metric is quoted early here and properly introduced in ch21.

Inverse vielbein components for the Schwarzschild static frame.
Diagonal vielbein and inverse for the spherical-coordinate metric of the fluid example.
Orthonormal basis 1-forms of a freely falling frame are also parallel transported.
Step-by-step 1-form argument (Leibniz rule plus parallel-transported coframe) for moving the vielbein inside the covariant derivative in Example 10.13.

notable.summary: For an open Robertson-Walker-type metric with scale factor a(t), convert a vector's components and a single component of a (1,2) tensor into the orthonormal frame.
notable.why_notable: Practises the one-vielbein-per-index rule on a cosmological metric ahead of ch16; the printed metric has sin^2 phi where sin^2 theta is meant.

notable.summary: Find the orthonormal-frame connection coefficients of the flat plane in polar coordinates without using vielbeins (they are not tensors), then check that their antisymmetric part equals the commutator of the frame vectors.
notable.why_notable: The only place in the chapter where non-coordinate connection coefficients are computed; exposes the index-ordering convention (answers: Gamma^rhat_{thetahat thetahat} = -1/r, Gamma^thetahat_{thetahat rhat} = 1/r).

notable.summary: A particle moves radially in a static spherically symmetric field with a given constant time component of its velocity 1-form; find its other components, its coordinate speed dr/dt, and the speed a local static observer measures.
notable.why_notable: Directly operationalizes the chapter's slogan that coordinates are not measurements; flagged by the authors as a warm-up for Part IV.

notable.summary: For an orthogonal coordinate system with diagonal metric, express the gradient and covariant divergence in orthonormal components and specialize to cylindrical and spherical polar coordinates.
notable.why_notable: Recovers the familiar scale-factor formulas of undergraduate vector calculus from the GR machinery.

notable.summary: Using the metric of a rotating frame, show that light sent between two points on the rim of a centrifuge suffers no frequency shift.
skills: static observers in a stationary metric
notable.why_notable: Applies observer-energy ideas to a non-diagonal metric; the full argument needs conservation of p_t (time-independent metric), which the chapter has not stated.

notable.summary: Given a Newman-Penrose null tetrad with its orthogonality and normalization conditions, write the local metric in that basis and find the dual basis 1-forms.
notable.why_notable: Shows that local frames need not be orthonormal; the local metric becomes off-diagonal.

notable.summary: Propose vielbein components for the 1+1 dimensional light-cone metric ds^2 = -du dv.
notable.why_notable: Forces the learner beyond the diagonal square-root recipe (e.g. via t = (u+v)/2, x = (v-u)/2).

exercises.solutions: Appendix E gives answers to Exercises 10.1, 10.2, 10.3, 10.5 and 10.6 (not 10.4 or 10.7).

difficulty.notes: The physical idea (measurements are projections onto an observer's frame, E = -p.u) is simple and well illustrated, and most examples use diagonal 2D metrics. Difficulty comes from dense index bookkeeping with hatted and unhatted indices, the proliferation of vielbein rules stated rather than motivated in the main text (proofs sit in margin notes), several printing slips (10.28, the summary's missing square, g_phiphi in note 14, sin^2 phi in Exercise 10.1), and a freely falling frame section that asserts rather than shows vanishing connection. Nothing beyond linear algebra and ch7 covariant derivatives is required.
