teaching_gems.gem: Energy measured by any observer is -p.u_obs, derived in one line from e_0hat = u and eta_00 = -1.
teaching_gems.why_effective: A single scalar formula replaces Lorentz transformations, Doppler formulas and gravitational redshift recipes, and it can be evaluated in whatever frame is easiest.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Universal 'what does this observer measure?' widget: pick a spacetime (Minkowski, Rindler, Schwarzschild), an emitter and a receiver world line; it computes -k.u at both ends and animates the photon with a colour shift.

teaching_gems.gem: An observer is a world line with a frame attached, time axis along the tangent (Fig. 10.2).
teaching_gems.why_effective: Turns the vague word 'observer' into a concrete geometric object that can be drawn, computed and compared.
teaching_gems.app_idea: World-line editor that attaches a live tetrad and shows how it tilts under acceleration and boosts.

teaching_gems.gem: Accelerated observer's frame by swapping cosh and sinh, and the resulting exponential redshift.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Short, fully explicit calculation that previews horizon redshift physics in flat spacetime with no curvature.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Rindler rocket simulator: learner sets g and watches received starlight redshift, plotting ln(omega) against tau as a straight line of slope -g.

teaching_gems.gem: Non-coordinate bases introduced through rotating polar unit vectors in the Kepler problem.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Anchors an abstract distinction in mechanics every physics learner has seen, and shows 'basis turning' terms before connection coefficients in GR.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Orbit tracer that splits the acceleration arrow into d(components)/dt and 'basis rotation' contributions.

teaching_gems.gem: For diagonal metrics the vielbein is just square roots of |g_mumu|, checked by contracting with g.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Gives a two-second recipe that covers most metrics met in the book (Schwarzschild, Robertson-Walker, spheres) and a check that catches mistakes.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Drag-in-a-metric card: diagonal entries produce vielbein and inverse instantly, with a green tick when g = e^T eta e checks.

teaching_gems.gem: Stationary versus freely falling frames as the two canonical observers, built for the same Schwarzschild geometry.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Juxtaposes a hovering and a falling observer at the same event, the key comparison for black-hole physics later.
teaching_gems.app_idea: t-r spacetime diagram near a black hole with static and infalling tetrads at a chosen r; slider in r shows the relative boost speed sqrt(2M/r) approaching 1 at the horizon and the static tetrad degenerating.

teaching_gems.gem: In a parallel-transported frame, covariant derivatives become ordinary derivatives of frame components (Example 10.13).
teaching_gems.why_effective: Justifies doing special-relativistic calculus inside a falling lab and sets up geodesic deviation as an ordinary ODE.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Toggle between coordinate-component and frame-component plots of a transported vector along a Schwarzschild geodesic: coordinate components wiggle, frame components stay flat.

teaching_gems.gem: Perfect-fluid tensor collapses to diag(rho, p, p, p) in the orthonormal frame.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Shows immediately why physicists quote densities and pressures in orthonormal frames: the coordinate scale factors are artefacts.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Side-by-side matrices of T in coordinate and orthonormal components as the learner moves a point in chi and theta.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Printed slips: eqn 10.28 has (e_rhat)^theta where (e_thetahat)^theta is meant; Example 10.5 calls the plane 'cylindrical-polar' and writes d phi^2 with coordinates (r, theta); Fig. 10.3 caption has 'which' for 'while'; the chapter summary writes g_00 (u^0) = -1 without the square; margin note 14 gives g_phiphi = r^2 sin theta instead of r^2 sin^2 theta; Exercise 10.1 has sin^2 phi for sin^2 theta; on p.111 the text says e_r and e_theta cannot be expanded in Cartesian derivatives where the normalized e_rhat and e_thetahat are meant; and Example 10.4 speaks of 'cylindrical coordinates' for what is a plane-polar problem.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Careful readers checking the algebra may lose confidence or copy wrong components.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Present corrected forms in the app and flag each slip briefly in tutor responses when a learner quotes the book.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Example 10.12 says '(e_rhat)^r = 1' is a choice, but once e_that = u and e_rhat lies in the t-r plane, orthogonality to u plus normalization forces (e_rhat)^r = +/-1; the orthogonality condition that fixes the sign of the t component is never written.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Learners may think vielbeins carry arbitrary free choices here, or get the sign of (e_rhat)^t wrong.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Write both conditions: g(u, e_rhat) = 0 gives (e_rhat)^t = -(2M/r)^{1/2}(1-2M/r)^{-1}(e_rhat)^r, then normalization gives (e_rhat)^r = 1.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: The claim that connection coefficients vanish along the geodesic in the freely falling frame is asserted; parallel transport of the tetrad only removes connection terms with the derivative along u, and the chapter never checks that Example 10.12's tetrad is actually parallel transported.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Learners may believe all frame connection coefficients vanish on the world line for any extension of the tetrad, and conflate the falling frame with Riemann normal or Fermi normal coordinates.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: State precisely: nabla_u e_alphahat = 0 means Gamma^muhat_{alphahat 0hat} = 0 along the curve; show quickly that nabla_u e_thetahat = 0 for radial infall (u^r d(1/r)/dr + (1/r)u^r Gamma^theta_{r theta} = 0); name Fermi normal coordinates as the full construction.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: The stationary-frame recipe is given without its domain: it needs g_00 < 0, and for non-diagonal metrics (Exercises 10.5, 10.7) the square-root rule fails.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Applying u^0 = (-g_00)^{-1/2} inside r = 2M or beyond a rotating frame's light cylinder yields imaginary results; learners stall on Exercise 10.7.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Add the condition g_00 < 0 and demonstrate Gram-Schmidt starting from e_0hat = u for a non-diagonal metric (the rotating frame is a good example).

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Index ordering of connection coefficients: ch7 writes the derivative index last (d e_mu/dx^alpha = Gamma^lambda_{mu alpha} e_lambda) while the commutator identity in Exercise 10.2(b) and its Appendix E answer treat the first lower index as the derivative direction.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: In a non-coordinate basis Gamma is not symmetric, so mixing conventions produces sign errors in the commutator check.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Fix one convention explicitly (e.g. nabla_{e_beta} e_alpha = Gamma^mu_{alpha beta} e_mu) and restate the identity in that convention before the exercise.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Exercise 10.5 relies on conservation of the covariant time component of photon momentum in a time-independent metric, which the chapter has not introduced.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: The one-line Appendix E answer ('same r, so same E') looks like it ignores the photon's travel through the gravitational-like potential.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Explain that a t-independent metric conserves p_t along geodesics, and static observers measure E = -p_t u^t, so equal u^t implies equal frequencies.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: No explicit example compares what two different observers measure at the same event, although this is the chapter's conceptual core.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Learners may treat frames as bookkeeping rather than as the physical distinction between, e.g., hovering and falling observers.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Add a worked comparison: -u_static.u_infall = (1-2M/r)^{-1/2} = gamma, giving relative speed sqrt(2M/r), and the different energies each assigns to the same photon.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Example 10.2 uses g both for the proper acceleration and for an unknown component function g(tau); Example 10.4 uses omega for angular velocity while Example 10.3 uses it for light frequency.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Symbol collisions invite algebra mistakes when solving (10.5)-(10.6).
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Rename the unknown functions (e.g. A(tau), B(tau)) and use theta-dot for angular speed.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: The margin argument in Example 10.13 invokes the covariant derivative of a scalar via 'the earlier sidenote' without pointing to where it was shown, and relies on the Leibniz rule for the pairing, which ch7 postpones to Part V.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: The key step (10.68) can feel like sleight of hand.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: State plainly: components chi^muhat = <omega^muhat, chi> are scalars; the covariant derivative of a scalar is its directional derivative; Leibniz plus nabla_u omega^muhat = 0 finishes the proof.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Newman-Penrose normalizations in Exercise 10.6 (l.n = 1, m.m-bar = -1) are those of a (+,-,-,-) signature, contrary to the book's (-,+,+,+); the Appendix E answer also contains index slips.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Learners in the book's signature may find the conditions inconsistent with real null vectors built from their eta.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Note the signature mismatch and give the (-,+,+,+) version (l.n = -1, m.m-bar = 1) as an alternative.

tutor_notes: Open with: 'If a metric has a coordinate called t, is t what your wristwatch reads?' Use the static Schwarzschild observer to show sqrt(-g_tt) dt is the proper time, which makes the Einstein quotation concrete.

Recommended order: vector versus components -> measurement as projection -> e_0hat = u -> E = -p.u (moving observer, accelerated observer) -> coordinate vs non-coordinate basis (polar unit vectors) -> vielbein as translation matrix -> diagonal square-root recipe -> Schwarzschild static frame -> freely falling frame and Example 10.13.
For novices, skip §10.2's formal rules at first: teach E = -p.u and the diagonal square-root recipe, then return to index-swap rules when the learner needs them (ch11 §11.7, Part IV).
Check for understanding: 'Two observers pass through the same event with different velocities. Do they agree on p? On p^0hat?' Expected: same vector, different components.
Check: ask the learner to derive E = gamma m from -p.u by evaluating in the particle's rest frame, and to explain why that shortcut is legitimate (the dot product is a scalar).

Check: give ds^2 = -(1+2 Phi) dt^2 + (1-2 Phi)(dx^2+dy^2+dz^2) and ask for the static vielbein; then ask what frequency a static observer at Phi measures for light that has frequency omega_inf far away (using conservation of p_t).

Common question: 'Why do we need non-coordinate bases at all?' Answer: measurements need orthonormal axes, and orthonormal axes in curved or curvilinear settings usually cannot come from any coordinate grid; the polar e_theta/r example and its non-zero commutator show this.

Common question: 'Is the vielbein unique?' Answer: no; any Lorentz transformation of the hatted index gives another valid frame; choosing an observer (u) fixes the boost and a spatial orientation fixes the rest.

Common question: 'Is the freely falling frame the same as the static frame?' Use Examples 10.10 and 10.12 at the same r and compute the relative speed sqrt(2M/r); emphasize static observers do not exist at r <= 2M.
Watch for sign errors with eta_00 = -1: learners often write E = p.u or forget that p_0hat = -p^0hat.
Watch for learners trying to transform connection coefficients with vielbeins (Exercise 10.2 hint); redirect to computing nabla_{e_betahat} e_alphahat directly.
Watch for missing hats: when a learner's result is off by metric factors, first ask which basis each index belongs to.
Bridge forward: Example 10.13's result is exactly what lets ch11 write geodesic deviation as d^2 xi^ihat/dtau^2 = -R^ihat_{0hat jhat 0hat} xi^jhat.
